'''Gorton:''' {{legend0|#ffb2b2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} {{legend0|#D72F30|70–80%}} | title = U.S. Senator | before_election = [[Slade Gorton]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Maria Cantwell]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsWA}} The '''2000 United States Senate election in Washington''' was held on November 7, 2000. Republican incumbent [[Slade Gorton]] ran for re-election to a fourth (and third consecutive{{Efn|Gorton had previously served one term in the Senate from 1981 to 1987. He lost re-election in 1986 and was elected to the Senate against in 1988.|name=priorterm}}) term in office but was narrowly defeated by U.S. representative [[Maria Cantwell]]. The race was the most expensive contest in [[Washington (state)|Washington state]] history at the time.{{Cite news |last=Ayres Jr |first=B. Drummond |date=October 19, 2000 |title=THE 2000 CAMPAIGN; CAMPAIGN BRIEFING |language=en-US |pages=31 |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/10/19/us/the-2000-campaign-campaign-briefing.html |access-date=2021-10-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211004042742/https://www.nytimes.com/2000/10/19/us/the-2000-campaign-campaign-briefing.html |archive-date=October 4, 2021 |issn=0362-4331}} By a margin of 0.09 percent of the vote, this election was the closest race of the [[2000 United States Senate elections|2000 Senate elections]]. Cantwell's victory was credited to her strength in the [[Seattle]] suburbs. She spent almost $10 million (approximately ${{Inflation|index=USD|value=10|start_year=2000|r=0|fmt=c}} million in {{Inflation/year|index=USD}} dollars) of her own money, which she had earned as an executive at [[RealNetworks]].{{Cite news |last=Egan |first=Timothy |date=November 23, 2000 |title=Cantwell Declared Washington Victor |language=en-US |pages=24 |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/11/23/us/cantwell-declared-washington-victor.html |access-date=October 4, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211004042744/https://www.nytimes.com/2000/11/23/us/cantwell-declared-washington-victor.html |archive-date=October 4, 2021 |issn=0362-4331}} {{As of|2026}}, this is the last time any U.S. senator from Washington lost re-election. == Blanket primary == === Candidates === ==== Democratic ==== * [[Maria Cantwell]], [[RealNetworks]] senior vice president and former U.S. representative from [[Seattle]] * [[Deborah Senn]], [[Washington State Office of the Insurance Commissioner|Washington insurance commissioner]] * Barbara Lampet, retired nurse and perennial candidate * Robert Tilden Medley ==== Republican ==== * [[Slade Gorton]], incumbent U.S. senator since 1989{{Efn|Gorton had previously served one term in the Senate from 1981 to 1987. He lost re-election in 1986 and was elected to the Senate against in 1988.|name=priorterm}} * Warren E. Hanson, [[commercial fishing|commercial fisherman]] * Ken McCandless * June Riggs ==== Libertarian ==== * Jeff Jared, attorney === Campaign === The primary campaign pitted Cantwell and Deborah Senn against each other for the Democratic nomination. Cantwell was generally considered the more moderate of the two, and touted her private sector success in Seattle's [[Dot-com bubble|booming technology industry]]. Senn was considered as a [[Populism in the United States|populist]] and campaigned as a staunch critic and opponent of the insurance industry.{{Cite web |last=Searcey |first=Dionne |date=September 14, 2000 |title=Cantwell, Senn contrast in style, share views |url=https://archive.seattletimes.com/archive/?date=20000914&slug=4042411 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211004042742/https://archive.seattletimes.com/archive/?date=20000914&slug=4042411 |archive-date=October 4, 2021 |access-date=October 4, 2021 |website=[[The Seattle Times]]}}{{Cite web |last=Ammons |first=David |date=August 27, 2000 |title=U.S. SENATE: Deborah Senn |url=https://products.kitsapsun.com/archive/2000/08-27/0016_u_s__senate__deborah_senn.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211004042746/https://products.kitsapsun.com/archive/2000/08-27/0016_u_s__senate__deborah_senn.html |archive-date=October 4, 2021 |access-date=October 4, 2021 |website=[[The Kitsap Sun]]}} ===Polling=== {| class="wikitable" style="font-size:90%;text-align:center;" |- valign=bottom ! He lost re-election in 1986 and was elected to the Senate against in 1988.|name=priorterm}} (Republican) === Campaign === In the general election, Cantwell campaigned as a modern candidate with experience in high tech who understood the modern economy and accused Gorton of offering "19th-century solutions to 21st-century problems." Gorton criticized Cantwell for spending millions on her own campaign, arguing she was trying to buy her way into the Senate. === Debates === *[https://www.c-span.org/video/?160132-1/washington-senatorial-debate Complete video of debate], October 30, 2000 === Endorsements === {{Endorsements box | title = Slade Gorton (R) | width = 50em | list = ;State senators *[[Tim Sheldon]], [[Washington's 35th legislative district|LD-35]] (1997–2023) ''(Democratic)''{{Cite web|url=https://www.heraldnet.com/2000/11/12/sheldons-decision-allows-democrats-to-maintain-slim-majority/|title=Sheldon’s decision allows Democrats to maintain slim majority|first=Archive|last=Imports|date=November 13, 2000}} }} {{Endorsements box | title = Maria Cantwell (D) | width = 50em | list = ;Newspapers *''[[The Seattle Times]]''{{Cite news|url=https://www.seattletimes.com/opinion/mike-mcgavick-for-us-senate/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240708041912/https://www.seattletimes.com/opinion/mike-mcgavick-for-us-senate/ |archive-date=2024-07-08 |url-status=live|title=Mike McGavick for U.S. Senate|quote=We endorsed Cantwell six years ago...|last=Editorial Board|first=The Seattle Times|date=October 22, 2006|work=[[The Seattle Times]]|access-date=November 14, 2025|url-access=subscription}} }} ===Polling=== {{#chart:2000 United States Senate election in Washington.chart}} {| class="wikitable" style="font-size:90%;text-align:center;" |- valign="bottom" ! scope="col" |Poll source ! scope="col" |Date(s) ! scope="col" style="width:75px;" |Sample

Elway Research|first=Nate|last=Silver|date=March 25, 2021|access-date=January 3, 2022|archive-date=May 22, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220522201010/https://projects.fivethirtyeight.com/pollster-ratings/elway-research/|url-status=dead}} |October 18–20, 2000 |400 (RV) |– | {{Party shading/Republican}} |'''46%''' |45% |7% |} === Results === The victor of the race was at first unclear due to the amount of absentee ballots; the certified count on November 22 reported that Cantwell was ahead by 1,953 votes.{{cite news |last1=Associated Press |date=December 2, 2000 |title=Recount Seals Senate Race In Washington For Democrat |pages=8 |work=New York Times |agency=Associated Press |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/12/02/us/recount-seals-senate-race-in-washington-for-democrat.html |access-date=February 9, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210165837/https://www.nytimes.com/2000/12/02/us/recount-seals-senate-race-in-washington-for-democrat.html |archive-date=February 10, 2021}} Following the recount, Cantwell was certified the winner of the election by 2,229 votes out of more than 2.4 million.{{cite web |last1=Ammons |first1=David |date=December 2, 2000 |title=CAMPAIGN 2000: U.S. Senate Race: It's final: Cantwell defeats Gorton |url=https://products.kitsapsun.com/archive/2000/12-02/0065_campaign_2000__u_s__senate_race__.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210214140832/https://products.kitsapsun.com/archive/2000/12-02/0065_campaign_2000__u_s__senate_race__.html |archive-date=February 14, 2021 |access-date=February 9, 2021 |website=Kitsap Sun}} Cantwell carried only five of the state's 39 counties, but won [[King County, Washington|King County]] (home to [[Seattle]]) by more than a 150,000-vote margin. The result was the second loss in Gorton's political career, after he lost re-election to a second Senate term in [[1986 United States Senate election in Washington|1986]]. Approximately 26,000 ballots were rejected during the recount for various issues.{{cite news |last=McCarthy |first=Sean L. |date=December 10, 2000 |title=Every vote counts? Her victory meant that both of Washington's senators were female (the other being [[Patty Murray]]); it was at that time one of three states to hold the distinction, along with California and Maine. Cantwell also became the thirteenth woman to serve in the Senate at the same time. Cantwell's election also meant that Democrats and Republicans would have a 50–50 tie in the Senate. At the time the race was called, it was still unclear whether [[Dick Cheney]] or [[Joe Lieberman]] would be [[Vice President of the United States|Vice President]] and thus cast the tie-breaking vote. At the time, it was noted that if the [[Al Gore 2000 presidential campaign|Gore-Lieberman]] ticket were victorious, then Connecticut's [[John G. Rowland|Republican governor]] would appoint Senator Lieberman's replacement, thereby giving Republicans a majority in the chamber; if the [[George W. Bush 2000 presidential campaign|Bush-Cheney ticket]] were elected (the ultimate outcome), with Cantwell the winner of her race, there would be a tie in the chamber. In a January 2002 appearance on [[C-SPAN]]'s ''[[Booknotes]]'', [[Ralph Nader]] (the 2000 [[Green Party of the United States|Green Party]] [[Ralph Nader 2000 presidential campaign|presidential nominee]]) stated that when he met with Democratic Senator [[Harry Reid]] after the election, Reid had credited his candidacy with aiding Cantwell's victory; Nader had received 103,000 votes in the state, and since the party didn't run a Senate candidate, his supporters backed Cantwell down the ballot.{{Cite episode | title = Crashing the Party | url = https://www.c-span.org/video/?168072-1/crashing-party | access-date = February 9, 2021 | series = Booknotes | first = Brian | last = Lamb | network = C-SPAN | date = February 4, 2002 | minutes = 20:40 | quote = And I met with Senator Harry Reid, the number two Democrat in the Senate. And he acknowledged that the Green spillover votes elected Maria Cantwell. She won by 2,300 votes. I got 103,000 in Washington state, and there was no Green Party Senate candidate.
